questions.stem: When moving out of home for the first time, which is an establishment cost rather than an ongoing cost?
options: Paying the weekly rent and buying groceries each week
Paying the electricity, gas and internet bills every quarter
Paying for the bus or train to and from work each day
Paying the rental bond and buying furniture
questions.explanation: Establishment costs are one-off costs of setting up, such as the bond, furniture, appliances and connection fees. Rent, food, bills and transport keep coming for as long as you live independently, so they are ongoing costs.

questions.stem: Which identification document is correctly matched with the organisation that issues it?
options: Medicare card: the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages
Australian passport: the Australian Taxation Office
Birth certificate: Services Australia, through Centrelink
Tax file number: the Australian Taxation Office
questions.explanation: The Australian Taxation Office issues tax file numbers. Medicare cards come from Services Australia, birth certificates from the state or territory Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, and passports from the Australian Passport Office.

questions.stem: Which type of car insurance is compulsory in every Australian state and territory, and covers injuries to other people in a crash?
options: Comprehensive car insurance
Third party, fire and theft car insurance
Compulsory third party (CTP) insurance
Third party property insurance
questions.explanation: Every registered vehicle must have compulsory third party insurance, which covers people injured or killed in a crash you cause. In NSW it is called a Green Slip. The other types are optional and cover damage to cars and property rather than injuries to people.

questions.stem: Tom has only third party property insurance. He causes a crash that damages his own car and another driver's car. What does his policy pay for?
options: Repairs to both cars, minus the excess he has to pay
Repairs to his own car, but not to the other driver's car
The other driver's injuries, but neither car's repairs
Repairs to the other driver's car, but not to his own
questions.explanation: Third party property insurance covers damage you cause to other people's cars and property, but not your own car; comprehensive insurance would cover both. Injuries to people are covered by compulsory third party insurance, not property insurance.

questions.stem: Which habit best helps a young adult build a good credit score?
options: Avoiding having any bills or accounts in their own name at all
Moving any unpaid bills into a friend's name before they fall due
Paying bills and loan repayments on time, every time
Applying for several credit cards to show lenders they are keen
questions.explanation: Credit reports record whether repayments are made on time, so a steady record of paying on time builds a good score that makes future loans easier and cheaper. Many credit applications in a short time count against you, and having no accounts leaves no history to judge.

questions.stem: Mia is 18, studying full-time and living away from home. Which Centrelink payment might she be able to receive?
options: Youth Allowance
Age Pension
Austudy
Carer Payment
questions.explanation: Youth Allowance supports eligible full-time students and apprentices aged 18 to 24, and some younger people, subject to income and assets tests. Austudy is the similar payment for students aged 25 and over, so it does not apply to an 18-year-old.

questions.stem: In a household budget, which of these is a fixed expense?
options: Rent of $300 a week set by a lease
Groceries bought each week
Electricity used over each three-month quarter
Going out with friends
questions.explanation: A fixed expense stays the same each period, like rent under a lease or a set phone plan. Groceries, electricity and entertainment change with how much you buy or use, so they are variable expenses and are where savings are usually found.

questions.stem: Sam's take-home pay is $800 a week. He spends $300 on rent, $150 on food, $60 on transport, $20 on his phone and $120 on entertainment. He wants to save $200 a week. How far short is his budget?
options: $70 a week
$50 a week
$150 a week
$200 a week
questions.explanation: His spending totals $300 + $150 + $60 + $20 + $120 = $650, which leaves $800 − $650 = $150 to save. That is $50 less than his $200 goal, so he must cut variable spending such as entertainment or lower his savings target.

questions.stem: A common guide says rent is affordable if it is no more than about 30 per cent of gross income. Ava earns $1,200 a week before tax. What is the most rent she should aim to pay?
options: $840 a week
$360 a week
$400 a week
$300 a week
questions.explanation: 30 per cent of $1,200 is 0.3 × $1,200 = $360. Paying much more than this can leave a household in housing stress, with too little left for food, transport and savings.

questions.stem: In NSW, when a tenant pays a rental bond, what must the landlord or agent do with it?
options: Lodge it with NSW Fair Trading, which holds it until the lease ends
Keep it in their own bank account and decide later how much to give back
Spend it on cleaning and repairs before the tenant moves in
Pay it to the local council as a deposit on the property's rates
questions.explanation: Bonds in NSW must be lodged with NSW Fair Trading, so neither side can simply keep the money. At the end of the tenancy it is returned to the tenant unless the landlord makes a claim for unpaid rent or damage.

questions.stem: Why should a new tenant fill in the condition report carefully and keep a copy?
options: It lets the tenant leave before the lease ends without giving any notice
It makes the tenant responsible for all repairs needed during the lease
It records damage already there, so the tenant is not charged for it when leaving
It fixes the rent so that it cannot be increased at any time during the whole lease
questions.explanation: The condition report is the evidence of the property's state at the start of the lease. If there is a dispute over the bond, it shows which marks and damage were there before the tenant moved in.

questions.stem: Josh and his landlord cannot agree on how much of his bond should be returned. In NSW, which body can make a binding decision?
options: The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)
The Fair Work Commission
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission
The Reserve Bank of Australia
questions.explanation: NCAT hears tenancy disputes, including claims on bonds, and its decisions must be followed. NSW Fair Trading can give advice and help the two sides talk, but it is the tribunal that decides.

questions.stem: Which is a landlord's responsibility rather than the tenant's?
options: Paying for damage that the tenant caused by being careless or rough
Paying the tenant's electricity and internet bills
Cleaning the property for the tenant every week
Fixing a hot water system that stops working through normal wear
questions.explanation: Landlords must keep the property in reasonable repair and arrange urgent repairs such as a broken hot water system. Tenants must keep the property reasonably clean and pay for damage they cause.

questions.stem: Which list contains only recurring (ongoing) costs of owning a car?
options: Purchase price, insurance and the transfer fee
Stamp duty, the transfer fee and roadside assistance
Fuel, servicing, insurance and yearly registration
Purchase price, stamp duty, fuel and servicing
questions.explanation: Recurring costs keep coming as long as you own the car: fuel, servicing, tyres, insurance and registration renewals. The purchase price, stamp duty and transfer fee are initial costs paid once when the car is bought.

questions.stem: Why can a three-year-old used car be better value than the same model bought new?
options: Stamp duty is charged only on new cars, never on cars sold second-hand
New cars lose much of their value in the first few years, and the second owner avoids that loss
Used cars do not need insurance or registration, so they are much cheaper to run every single year
Used cars are covered by a longer warranty from the maker than brand-new cars are
questions.explanation: Depreciation is steepest in a car's early years, so the first owner absorbs the biggest fall in value. A used car still needs insurance and registration, and stamp duty applies whenever a car changes hands.

questions.stem: Two flatmates buy a fridge together, sharing the cost equally. What is the main risk of this joint ownership?
options: A jointly owned item cannot be sold until both owners turn 25
They may disagree about who keeps it, or who pays whom, when one moves out
Jointly owned goods are not covered by the consumer guarantees under the law
Both flatmates must pay GST on the fridge again each year they own it
questions.explanation: Sharing a purchase cuts each person's cost, but it needs a clear agreement about what happens if the household splits up. Consumer guarantees still apply to the fridge however many people paid for it.

questions.stem: Which is the most likely consequence of repeatedly missing loan repayments?
options: The lender must offer a lower interest rate to make the repayments easier
A default on the credit report and debt collectors, making future borrowing harder
The debt is cancelled automatically after three repayments have been missed
The lender must stop charging any interest until the borrower is able to start paying again
questions.explanation: Missed repayments bring late fees and extra interest, and a default can stay on a credit report for years. Unpaid debts can be passed to debt collectors and, in serious cases, lead to bankruptcy, so asking the lender early for a hardship arrangement is the better path.

questions.stem: Instead of buying a car, Zoe uses a car-share service a few times a month. What is the main financial advantage?
options: The government pays her a rebate for each trip because she does not own a car of her own
She pays only when she uses a car, avoiding insurance, registration and depreciation
Car-share services are free for drivers under 25 who hold a full licence
She earns income from the car-share company every time she drives one of its cars
questions.explanation: The sharing economy lets people pay for access instead of ownership, which suits someone who drives rarely. A car owner pays large fixed costs, such as insurance, registration and loss of value, even when the car sits unused.
